chapter: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
title: Fletcher Henderson and Duke Ellington ignoring band grievances
summary: Collins compares Henderson to Ellington, both indifferent to personal squabbles as long as the music was played, citing the 1951 Big Show.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: and Fletcher was. Fletcher reminded me a lot of Duke, and --

Well, he was primarily -- he as a great piano player, but he was primarily a writer. And he wrote for individuals, different individuals in his band. And personalities never bothered him. You know, they could all have their personal grievances, and things, but it never -- it went all over Fletcher's head. Because the thing to Fletcher was music, and to hear his music played. And Duke was a lot like this.
Well, Duke would dabble in personalities.
Yeah, but I wanted to say is I noticed the time that I was travelling with Duke, when I was with Nat, that --

The Big Show in 1951, I believe. Some of the guys would disappear for days, and when they would show up Duke would never acknowledge their absence. It didn't make any difference to him, all he wanted was that his music be played. He was just-- I'd see the guys get furious over him over some imagined grievance, and they would rave and do -- Duke it just went right over his head. He would smile and -- Fletcher was a lot like this, you know. Whatever happened with these guys, he just never let it affect him. He loved
them and all this but he never got upset, at least I didn't see him get upset, and this way he reminded me a lot of Duke. And he was -- Fletcher was a great writer, you know.
